questions.q: Why is a slow (thermal) neutron more effective than a fast neutron at causing fission in uranium-235?
options: A fast neutron carries too little energy to disturb the nucleus
A neutron has no charge, so it needs no speed to enter; moving slowly it lingers near the nucleus long enough to be captured, giving a larger reaction cross-section
A slow neutron is attracted electrostatically to the positive nucleus
Fast neutrons are reflected by the metal's surface before reaching the nucleus
questions.explanation: Because the neutron is uncharged it is not repelled by the nucleus, so it does not need speed to get in. A slow neutron lingers near the nucleus long enough to be captured — a larger reaction cross-section — whereas a fast neutron tends to glance off or recoil away.

questions.q: In the liquid drop model, which two competing influences determine whether an excited uranium nucleus splits?
options: Gravity pulling inward versus the strong force pushing outward
The strong nuclear force acting like surface tension to hold the drop together, versus the electrostatic repulsion between protons pushing it apart
Neutron pressure versus proton pressure
Magnetic attraction versus electrostatic attraction
questions.explanation: The strong nuclear force behaves like surface tension pulling the drop back into a sphere, while the electrostatic repulsion between protons pushes it apart. As the wobbling nucleus stretches, the long-range repulsion between the two ends starts to win, and past a critical point the drop necks and splits.

questions.q: On the curve of binding energy per nucleon versus nucleon number, why does splitting uranium release energy?
options: Uranium sits at the peak of the curve, so splitting it climbs even higher
The fission fragments sit higher on the curve (closer to the iron-56 peak) than uranium, so they are more tightly bound and the surplus binding energy is released
The fragments are less tightly bound than uranium, releasing the difference
Splitting uranium creates new mass, which is converted to energy
questions.explanation: Uranium sits far out on the right-hand slope at about 7.5 MeV per nucleon. Its fragments (barium, krypton) sit nearer the iron-56 peak at around 8.5 MeV per nucleon, so they are more tightly bound. That extra total binding energy — the larger mass defect — is what gets released.

questions.q: What does the multiplication factor k represent, and what value corresponds to a steadily running power reactor?
options: The number of neutrons released per fission; k must exceed 3
The average number of neutrons from each fission that go on to cause another fission; a steady reactor holds k exactly equal to 1 (critical)
The ratio of fast to slow neutrons; a reactor needs k less than 1
The fraction of uranium-235 in the fuel; a reactor needs k above 90%
questions.explanation: k is the average number of neutrons from each fission that cause a further fission — the survival rate of the chain. k < 1 is subcritical (dies out), k = 1 is critical (steady reactor), and k > 1 is supercritical (grows exponentially, the bomb regime).

questions.q: Counterintuitively, adding a moderator such as graphite or water speeds up the chain reaction. Why?
options: The moderator adds extra neutrons to the core
The moderator slows fast fission neutrons to thermal speeds, and slow neutrons cause fission far more readily than fast ones
The moderator absorbs the slow neutrons that would otherwise stop the reaction
The moderator reflects escaping neutrons back into the core
questions.explanation: Fission neutrons emerge fast, but slow neutrons are far better at causing fission. The moderator's light atoms (carbon, hydrogen) let neutrons bounce off and lose energy with each collision, slowing them to thermal speeds — so slowing the neutrons down actually speeds the chain reaction up. Absorbing spare neutrons is the job of the control rods, not the moderator.

questions.q: Why is it physically impossible for a commercial power reactor to detonate like an atomic bomb?
options: Reactors contain no fissile material at all

Reactor fuel is enriched to only about 3-5% uranium-235, so the chain cannot grow explosively — the neutrons are mostly absorbed by uranium-238 before a runaway can build, whereas a bomb needs over 90% enrichment
Control rods make a nuclear detonation chemically impossible regardless of fuel
Reactor uranium is a different element from bomb uranium
questions.explanation: A bomb needs the chain to grow explosively in a millionth of a second, which requires over 90% enrichment. At the 3-5% enrichment of reactor fuel the chain cannot grow fast enough — neutrons are mostly absorbed by non-fissile uranium-238. A reactor can suffer a meltdown or steam explosion, but not a nuclear detonation.

questions.q: From memory, in your own words: explain where the ~200 MeV released in a single fission event actually comes from.
keyPoints: The mass of a nucleus is slightly less than the sum of its separate protons and neutrons — this missing mass is the mass defect, whose energy equivalent is the binding energy.
The fission products are more tightly bound than the original uranium, so the total products weigh slightly less than the reactants; that vanished mass is converted to energy.
Using Einstein's E = mc^2 (1 u = 931.5 MeV), the missing mass becomes energy, mostly the kinetic energy of the two fragments flying apart, totalling about 200 MeV per event.
questions.explanation: If you recalled mass defect, that the products are more tightly bound and slightly lighter than the reactants, and that the missing mass converts to energy via E = mc^2, grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: From memory: state the essential components of a controlled fission reactor and the problem each one solves.
keyPoints: Fuel: uranium enriched in fissile uranium-235 (natural uranium is only ~0.72% U-235).
Moderator (graphite or water): slows fast neutrons to thermal speeds, where they cause fission far more readily.
Control rods (cadmium, boron or hafnium): absorb spare neutrons to lower the multiplication factor — the throttle and brake.
Coolant to carry heat away, a reflector to bounce escaping neutrons back in, and shielding (concrete and lead) to absorb gamma rays and stray neutrons.
questions.explanation: If you named fuel, moderator, control rods and coolant/reflector/shielding with the job of each (especially moderator = slow down, control rods = absorb), grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: A fission reaction loses about 0.186 atomic mass units of mass. Using 1 u = 931.5 MeV, find the energy released from this mass defect.
questions.explanation: Multiplying the mass defect by the 931.5 MeV/u conversion factor gives about 173 MeV, carried mostly as the kinetic energy of the two fission fragments. Adding the gamma rays and the later radioactive decay of the fragments brings the total to roughly 200 MeV per fission event.

questions.q: Burning one atom of carbon releases about 10 eV; a single fission releases about 200 MeV. How many times more energy does fission release per atom?
questions.explanation: Fission delivers about twenty million times more energy per atom than a chemical reaction — which is why nuclear energy is in a different universe from chemical energy. One kilogram of fully fissioned uranium-235 releases roughly the energy of 20,000 tonnes of TNT.
